questions.title: Why could the Ninth Circuit stay the district court's preliminary injunctions before issuing its full merits opinion?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture here. The panel says it heard expedited argument, that a full opinion will come later, but in the meantime this order itself "shall constitute a stay pending appeal." How is the court able to effectively decide major parts of the case through a stay order before releasing the full opinion? Is this just an application of the normal Nken v. Holder stay factors, or does it mean the panel has already substantially decided the merits?

questions.title: How does 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) let the President suspend refugee admissions if Congress already created a refugee admissions scheme?
questions.question_body: The court seems to say Trump v. Hawaii basically controls the challenge to the executive order suspending refugee admissions, because § 1182(f) gives the President broad power to suspend the entry of a class of aliens. But the plaintiffs argued this conflicts with the Refugee Act of 1980, which appears to establish an ongoing statutory refugee system. I'm having trouble understanding the interaction between those two laws. Why doesn't the more specific refugee statute limit the President's general § 1182(f) power, at least as to refugees?

questions.title: What exactly is the legal difference between suspending refugee 'entry' and defunding refugee resettlement services after admission?
questions.question_body: The panel says the government is likely to win as to suspending refugee admissions, but not likely to win on at least one APA challenge involving reception and placement services for refugees already admitted to the U.S. I'm confused why these are treated as legally distinct. If the executive has broad discretion over refugee admissions, why doesn't that also carry over to stopping the domestic side of the refugee program? Is the key distinction that one issue concerns admission of noncitizens outside the country, while the other concerns statutory duties owed to people already admitted?

questions.title: Why is the funding issue framed as an APA claim instead of just a direct statutory violation under 8 U.S.C. § 1522?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the plaintiffs challenged the defunding of USRAP under the Administrative Procedure Act, and then the panel analyzes whether § 1522 requires the government to provide certain services. I'm not understanding why the APA is the vehicle here. If the statute itself allegedly mandates reception and placement services, why isn't the claim simply that the government violated the Refugee Act? Is the idea that terminating the cooperative agreements is final agency action that is unlawful because it is contrary to law under the APA?

questions.title: Does 8 U.S.C. § 1522 actually require refugee services, or does it merely authorize them?
questions.question_body: This seems to be the core disagreement between the majority and Judge Lee, and I'm struggling with the statutory interpretation. The majority relies on phrases like the Director "shall" provide certain things "to the extent of available appropriations," plus other subsections requiring action for unaccompanied minors and support projects. Judge Lee responds that the section is titled as an "Authorization," that subsections (b)-(e) repeatedly say the Director is "authorized" to provide assistance, and that subsection (a) only supplies conditions if the government chooses to fund programs. In statutes like this, how do courts decide whether "shall" creates a mandatory duty when surrounding text sounds discretionary?

questions.title: Why did the panel order reinstatement of cooperative agreements instead of just requiring the government to provide services by some other means?
questions.question_body: The opinion says § 1522 services may be provided through contracts, grants, or cooperative agreements, and then directs the government to reinstate whatever cooperative agreements are necessary to provide the required services. But if the statute only requires services to be provided, why can the court effectively tell the executive what contracting mechanism to use? Is this because the government admitted it had no replacement provider ready, so reinstatement was the only practical way to preserve compliance?

questions.title: What does it mean that the government's emergency motion was denied as moot after the court vacated and replaced its earlier stay orders?
questions.question_body: The order vacates the administrative stay from July 18 and also vacates the earlier March 25 stay (as later amended), then issues a new stay pending appeal. It also says the government's July 17 emergency motion to enforce, clarify, or amend the stay is denied as moot. I'm confused about why that motion became moot rather than being granted or denied on the merits. Is it simply because the old stay order that the motion was about no longer exists, so there is nothing left to clarify or enforce?
